newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lazard declines comment on partner's reported exit.
newsitem.headline: Lazard declines comment on partner's reported exit.

text.p: Lazard Freres would not comment on Wednesday on a newspaper report that the man once seen as likely to take charge of the blue-chip French merchant bank had left to begin a new career.

The afternoon daily Le Monde said Edouard Stern, who is a son-in-law of Lazard chairman Michel David-Weill, ceased on Tuesday to be a managing partner at Lazard Freres et Cie in Paris and of Lazard New York.
It said Stern would set up a new investment company which would receive $300 million out of a total $600 million capital from Lazard holdings Eurafrance and Gaz et Eaux.
Eurafrance said in a statement it would subscribe $225 million to the venture which would be headed by Stern and which would invest in companies, mainly overseas.
Gaz et Eaux would put up $75 million and the remaining $300 million would be staked by a group of investors led by Stern.
"The bank is not commenting," on the Le Monde report, said a spokesman at the traditionally secretive bank. But a person close to the bank said there was no reason to disbelieve it.
Stern's reported departure follows denials by David-Weill last January of reports of a succession crisis at the investment firm with operations in Paris, New York and London.
David-Weill also at the time rejected suggestions that he had ever anointed his son-in-law to succeed him.
David-Weill's family has dominated the transatlantic firm for four generations but none of his four daughters has shown an interest in banking.

Le Monde quoted David-Weill as saying he retained a "great affection" for Stern, 42, and that "his great talent is as an investor. He is much more gifted as a businessman...This will now be his principal activity."

He said that to show that there was "no misunderstanding or hard feelings, Stern will remain a silent partner in Lazard Freres et Cie but without a management role (and) will still have a capital stake."
Talk that Stern, who is married to David-Weill's eldest daughter, was being groomed to take the reins of the merchant bank had been rife ever since he joined in 1992.
Stern was said to have aroused antagonism in fellow partners because of what the media described as an abrasive manner.

But Le Monde said Stern was also seen as one of the few people able to act as a counterweight to the "old guard" at the bank and force it to take up new opportunities. Lazard faces growing competition from U.S. investment banks in the French market.
The newspaper said the bank had also recently lost another partner, Francois Fournier, "reinforcing the weight of the old guard".

David-Weill, 64, suggested recently in a U.S. magazine that the Lazard group had grown so big he was unsure it could be run by one man. One idea, he said, would be to have a directorate at each centre.
As for his own retirement, David-Weill has said he still has a number of years ahead of him. Under the bank's statutes, he can remain at the helm for another eight years.
The three Lazard houses, grouped under Lazard Partners, work mainly in corporate advisory services, including mergers and acquisitions and asset management.
